title: 23 — Design a Distributed Email Service
html:
23 — Design a Distributed Email Service

The one idea: email is three different workloads that need three different stores: metadata (folders, read flags, per-user queries) in a wide-column store partitioned by user; bodies and attachments in object storage; search in a dedicated index. Sending and receiving run through queues with SMTP workers at the edge.

Step 1 — Scope

  • 1 billion users; send/receive, fetch all emails, filter by read/unread, search by subject/sender/body, anti-spam and anti-virus.
  • Users connect with web/mobile clients over HTTP (not IMAP/POP for this design).
  • Reliability (no lost mail), availability, scalability, flexibility for new features.

Estimates

  • Send: 1B × 10 emails/day ÷ 10^5 ≈ 100,000 QPS.
  • Receive: 40 emails/user/day; metadata ~50 KB → 1B × 40 × 50 KB × 365 ≈ 730 PB/year of metadata.
  • 20% of emails have attachments, avg 500 KB → ~1,460 PB/year of attachments.

Step 2 — High-level design

Protocols background

  • SMTP — sending between mail servers.
  • POP / IMAP — traditional retrieval (IMAP keeps mail on the server).
  • HTTPS / JMAP — modern web/mobile clients.
  • DNS MX records — which server receives mail for a domain.

title: Email service — send and receive pipelines
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph Send
        C1["Client"] -->|HTTPS| WS["Web servers<br/>(auth, validation, rate limits)"]
        WS --> OQ["Outgoing queue"]
        OQ --> SMTPout["SMTP outgoing workers<br/>(spam/virus check, retry)"]
        SMTPout --> Ext["Internet"]
        WS --> SF[("Sent folder<br/>metadata")]
    end
    subgraph Receive
        Ext2["Internet"] --> LB["LB"] --> SMTPin["SMTP servers<br/>(accept/reject)"]
        SMTPin --> IQ["Incoming queue"]
        IQ --> MP["Mail processing workers<br/>(spam, virus, filters)"]
        MP --> Store[("Metadata DB + blob store + search index")]
        MP --> RT["Real-time servers<br/>(WebSocket)"] --> C2["Online client"]
    end

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Metadata database

Characteristics: headers small and hot; bodies large and read once-ish; mostly recent mail accessed; per-user queries only; must never lose data.

Options:

Option Verdict
Relational Great for search/joins but not for PB-scale blobs and this write rate
Distributed object storage Great for bodies/attachments; bad for flags and search
NoSQL wide-column (Bigtable-style) ✅ for metadata — partition by user, sort by time

Schema idea (partition key first):

folders_by_user      PK user_id → (folder_id, name)
emails_by_folder     PK (user_id, folder_id), clustering email_id DESC (TIMEUUID) → subject, from, preview, is_read
email_by_id          PK email_id → body ref, attachments refs
unread_emails        PK (user_id, folder_id), clustering email_id DESC      -- denormalised for "unread" filter

"Filter by unread" in a NoSQL store = denormalise into separate tables (NoSQL can't cheaply filter on a non-key column).

3.2 Consistency trade-off

Mailbox state must be correct (a message moved to trash must not appear in inbox), so choose consistency over availability for a mailbox: a single primary per mailbox; during failover the mailbox is briefly unavailable.

3.3 Email deliverability (for outgoing)

  • Dedicated IPs, warm them up gradually; classify bulk vs transactional mail on separate IPs.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC authentication.
  • Ban spammers quickly; handle feedback loops (complaints) and bounces.

3.4 Search

Needs full-text search over headers and bodies, per user, with lots of writes (every received email) and relatively few reads.

Option Pros Cons
Elasticsearch (index per user, routed by user_id) Mature, fast to build Another system to keep in sync (via Kafka)
Custom LSM-based search in the store Tuned for write-heavy workload Big engineering investment

Small/medium scale → Elasticsearch fed from the processing pipeline.

3.5 Scalability and availability

  • Per-user partitioning makes everything shard naturally.
  • Replicate across data centres; users served from their home DC.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Fault tolerance of each queue and worker, compliance (GDPR data deletion across all three stores), security (phishing protection, safe browsing, encryption at rest), and optimisations like attachment dedup by hash.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Metadata: Cosmos DB partitioned by userId (hierarchical partition keys: userId/folderId), or Azure Table Storage for cost.
  • Bodies/attachments: Blob Storage with content hash names for dedup; lifecycle policies to cool tier.
  • Search: Azure AI Search with an index per tenant or a userId filter + security trimming.
  • Queues: Service Bus for incoming/outgoing pipelines with DLQ for undeliverable mail.
  • Sending: Azure Communication Services Email for transactional mail; SMTP handling with MailKit in .NET.
  • Real-time new-mail push: SignalR.

Review checklist

  • Protocols (SMTP/IMAP/HTTP, MX) briefly.
  • Separate send and receive pipelines with queues.
  • Three stores: metadata (wide-column), blobs, search.
  • Denormalised tables for read/unread filters.
  • Deliverability: SPF/DKIM/DMARC, IP warm-up.
  • Consistency over availability per mailbox.
